good_cases.claim: The monk sets aside sensual desire and unskillful states, then enters a state of rapture and pleasure born of that withdrawal.
A virtuous monk lives by the code of monastic training rules, careful even about minor faults.
One who holds that the result of an action is shaped by how the deed was done can live the holy life and end suffering.
good_cases.note: indirect: the passage states this as one side of a contrast

good_cases.claim: Heedfulness is said to be the root and the highest of every skillful quality.
good_cases.note: direct restatement of the passage's second half

good_cases.claim: The speaker was startled into urgent spiritual effort by words from their mother.
good_cases.note: paraphrase of saṁvega, Pali hinge word untranslated in source

good_cases.claim: Telling a deliberate lie without any shame shows someone is barely a contemplative at all.
Monks are instructed to keep their conduct impeccable under the code of monastic rules, mindful of even trivial faults.
A monk who keeps the precepts carefully but is reborn among the devas, then returns to this world, is called one 'fettered inside.'
good_cases.note: long passage, claim covers its whole arc

good_cases.claim: An unwholesome state of mind brings suffering the way a cart wheel follows the ox that pulls it.
A calm and bright state of mind is followed by happiness, the way a shadow never leaves its owner.
In the first stage of this practice, a monk stays mindfully aware of the body, working to set aside craving and aversion toward the world.
good_cases.note: single-sentence list-style passage (project's known weak chunk type)

good_cases.claim: A deity radiant enough to light up the entire grove approached the Buddha at night and asked him about liberation.
good_cases.note: narrative passage, claim covers the frame story not the teaching

bad_case_controls.claim: The monk breaks the precept against killing.
The Buddha praised lying as a skillful quality.
bad_case_controls.note: states the opposite of the passage

bad_case_controls.claim: The best way to cook rice is to steam it slowly.
Jhāna is the ultimate goal described in this passage.
bad_case_controls.note: topically adjacent (meditation), but the passage never says this

bad_case_controls.claim: A pure heart leads to happiness.
bad_case_controls.note: true of the very next verse (DHP1:4), not this one — same source, wrong verse

bad_case_controls.claim: This passage describes someone who has fully ended the cycle of rebirth.
bad_case_controls.note: related vocabulary (rebirth), wrong outcome: a returner, not an arahant
